key_findings: Reasoning gains from CoT emerge with model scale; small models do not benefit comparably.
Few-shot exemplars containing intermediate steps are sufficient - no fine-tuning required.
Improvements span arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning tasks.
limitations: Gains are scale-dependent and were demonstrated on 2022-era models.
Few-shot exemplar selection is a hidden hyperparameter.
No mechanism is given for why intermediate tokens help; later work (e.g. faithfulness studies) questions whether the stated chain reflects the actual computation.
sources.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
sources.summary: Shows that prompting with a few worked examples containing intermediate reasoning steps ('chain of thought') substantially improves complex reasoning in sufficiently large language models. Reports state-of-the-art GSM8K accuracy for a 540B-parameter model prompted with eight exemplars, surpassing fine-tuned GPT-3 with a verifier.
sources.key_contribution: Introduced and empirically characterised chain-of-thought prompting as a scale-dependent emergent capability.

key_findings: On Game of 24, GPT-4 with chain-of-thought solved 4% of tasks versus 74% with Tree of Thoughts.
Deliberate search over thoughts beats token-level greedy decoding on tasks needing planning.
Also evaluated on Creative Writing and Mini Crosswords.
limitations: Large increase in inference cost (many LM calls per problem).
Requires a task-specific thought decomposition and evaluator prompt.
Results reported on 2023-era GPT-4; newer reasoning models internalise part of this.
sources.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
sources.summary: Generalises chain-of-thought from a single left-to-right chain to a tree of intermediate 'thoughts', allowing the model to explore multiple reasoning paths, self-evaluate states, look ahead and backtrack. NeurIPS 2023 camera-ready.
sources.key_contribution: Framed LM inference as search over a tree of thoughts with model-generated state evaluation, enabling lookahead and backtracking.

verification.notes: Primary source confirmed 2026-09-15; arXiv comment states 'NeurIPS 2023 camera ready version'

key_findings: Interleaving reasoning and acting reduces hallucination versus reasoning alone.
Only 1-2 in-context examples are needed to induce the behaviour.
Trajectories are more human-interpretable than action-only baselines.
limitations: Depends on a usable external tool/API; without grounding the benefit shrinks.
Error propagation still occurs when an early action is wrong.
Reported on 2022-2023 models.
sources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
sources.summary: Interleaves generated reasoning traces with task-specific actions so the model can both plan and query external sources. On HotpotQA and Fever, ReAct reduces the hallucination and error propagation typical of pure chain-of-thought by grounding in a Wikipedia API; on ALFWorld and WebShop it beats imitation and RL baselines by 34% and 10% absolute success rate with one or two in-context examples.
sources.key_contribution: Established the reasoning+acting loop that nearly all modern tool-using agents inherit.

verification.notes: Primary source confirmed 2026-09-15; v3 is the ICLR camera-ready. NOTE: OpenAlex returned a mismatched title for this DOI on the same date.

key_findings: Sampling many reasoning paths and majority-voting the answer beats greedy single-chain decoding.
The gain is largest on arithmetic and commonsense benchmarks.
Works without any additional training or verifier model.
limitations: Multiplies inference cost by the number of sampled chains.
Requires a well-defined, comparable final answer (voting is hard for open-ended output).
sources.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
sources.summary: Samples multiple diverse chain-of-thought reasoning paths from the same model and marginalises over them to select the most consistent final answer, rather than taking a single greedy decoding.
sources.key_contribution: Introduced self-consistency decoding: ensemble over reasoning paths, vote over answers.

key_findings: Linguistic self-reflection stored in episodic memory improves subsequent attempts.
No gradient updates are required - learning happens in-context.
Depends on a usable feedback signal (self-evaluation, unit tests, environment reward).
limitations: Needs a reliable feedback signal; weak feedback produces weak reflections.
Memory buffer grows with trials, adding context cost.
Self-evaluation can be systematically wrong, compounding errors.
sources.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
sources.summary: Agents verbally reflect on task feedback and store those reflections in an episodic memory buffer to condition future trials, improving performance without updating model weights.
sources.key_contribution: Introduced 'verbal reinforcement learning': reflection text as the learning signal.

key_findings: Pure RL (no supervised reasoning traces) is sufficient to produce long, self-verified reasoning.
Emergent behaviours observed: self-reflection, verification, strategy switching mid-chain.
Outperforms models trained with supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations on verifiable tasks.
Peer-reviewed: Nature volume 645, pages 633-638 (2025).
limitations: Gains are concentrated on verifiable tasks with automatic reward signals.
Very long reasoning traces increase latency and token cost substantially.
The released repository (deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1) has had no push in 445 days as of 2026-09-15: it is a published artifact, not an actively developed SDK.
sources.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
sources.summary: Demonstrates that reasoning ability can be elicited by pure reinforcement learning without human-labelled reasoning trajectories. Reports emergent behaviours including self-reflection, verification of intermediate steps, and dynamic strategy adaptation, with strong results on verifiable maths, coding-competition and STEM tasks. Published in Nature 645:633-638 (2025); arXiv v2 revised 4 Jan 2026.
sources.key_contribution: Showed reasoning can be incentivised rather than imitated, and released open checkpoints plus the recipe.

key_findings: Optimally allocated test-time compute can beat a model ~14x larger on some tasks.
The best strategy depends on prompt difficulty: easy prompts favour fewer samples, hard prompts favour search/verification.
Compute-optimal scaling requires a difficulty-aware policy, not a fixed budget.
limitations: Results depend on the availability of a verifier or reward signal.
Latency and cost grow with the compute multiplier.
Difficulty estimation is itself a model call and can be wrong.
sources.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
sources.summary: Studies how to spend extra compute at inference time - revising responses, searching over candidate solutions, or verifying with a learned verifier - and how to allocate that compute adaptively to question difficulty.
sources.key_contribution: Established test-time compute as a first-class scaling axis alongside parameter count.

key_findings: Human 92% vs GPT-4+plugins 15% at publication - a large, interpretable gap.
Questions are short and have unambiguous answers, making automatic scoring feasible.
Deliberately departs from the trend of benchmarking on tasks that are hard for humans.
limitations: Leaderboard numbers depend heavily on the scaffolding/agent used, not just the model.
466 questions is small enough that per-question variance matters.
Public split is exposed to training-data contamination over time.
sources.title: GAIA: a benchmark for General AI Assistants
sources.summary: 466 real-world questions that are conceptually simple for humans but hard for AI, requiring reasoning, multimodality handling, web browsing and general tool-use proficiency. Human respondents reach 92% while GPT-4 equipped with plugins reached 15% at publication.
sources.key_contribution: Provided a contamination-resistant, human-grounded benchmark for general AI assistants.

key_findings: Position of relevant information matters as much as its presence.
Performance degrades in the middle of long contexts (U-shaped curve).
Longer inputs hurt even explicitly long-context models.
Implication for agents: put critical instructions and evidence at the start or end, not buried mid-context.
limitations: Studied 2023-era models; newer architectures have narrowed but not eliminated the effect.
Tasks are retrieval-flavoured (multi-doc QA, KV retrieval); results may not transfer to code-heavy contexts.
Does not separate attention-pattern causes from training-data causes.
sources.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
sources.summary: Analyses multi-document QA and key-value retrieval and finds a U-shaped performance curve: models perform best when the relevant information is at the beginning or end of the context and degrade significantly when it sits in the middle. Performance also falls as total context length grows, even for models advertised as long-context.
sources.key_contribution: Quantified positional sensitivity in long contexts and supplied evaluation protocols for long-context models.
